title: Pattern and base words

facts.quote: Continuation Pattern A type of chart pattern that occurs in the middle of an existing trend. The previous trend resumes when the pattern is complete.
facts.claim: A continuation pattern forms in the middle of a trend, and the old trend resumes once it completes.

facts.quote: Continuation When price enters and exits a chart pattern in the same direction.
facts.claim: Bulkowski defines a continuation as price entering and leaving a pattern in the same direction.

facts.quote: Reversal Pattern A chart pattern that occurs before an existing trend reverses direction.
facts.claim: A reversal pattern forms before the trend turns the other way.

facts.quote: Reversal When price enters and exits a chart pattern in opposite directions.
facts.claim: Bulkowski defines a reversal as price entering and leaving a pattern in opposite directions.

facts.quote: Just because a pattern forms after a significant advance or decline does not mean it is a reversal pattern.
facts.claim: A pattern that forms after a big move is not automatically a reversal.

facts.quote: Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be classified as either reversal or continuation.
facts.claim: Many patterns, such as a rectangle, can be either a reversal or a continuation.

facts.quote: A pattern is not complete or activated until an actual breakout occurs
facts.claim: Fidelity's pattern guide: a pattern is not complete or activated until price actually breaks out.

facts.quote: Confirmation The price at which squiggles on a chart become a valid chart pattern. Usually occurs when price breaks out of the chart pattern trendline boundary.
facts.claim: Confirmation is the price where a shape becomes a valid pattern, usually the breakout through its boundary.

facts.quote: As with the symmetrical triangle, the rectangle pattern is incomplete until a breakout occurs.
facts.claim: A rectangle, like a symmetrical triangle, is incomplete until price breaks out.

facts.quote: A wedge pattern can be either a continuation or a reversal.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a wedge can be either a continuation or a reversal.

facts.quote: Measure rule A method, usually using the chart pattern height, to determine the minimum price move after a breakout
facts.claim: The measure rule uses the pattern's height to estimate a minimum move after the breakout.

facts.quote: Often that's the height added to or subtracted from the breakout price. It is an estimate only.
facts.claim: A pattern's price target is usually its height added to or taken from the breakout price, and it is only an estimate.

facts.quote: The measure rule computation varies from pattern to pattern and is usually inaccurate.
facts.claim: Bulkowski calls the measure rule usually inaccurate.

facts.quote: Any price target should serve as a rough guide, and other factors should also be considered.
facts.claim: StockCharts: any pattern price target is a rough guide.

facts.quote: Stick with original price targets of patterns after conditions have changed
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide lists sticking with a pattern's original target after conditions change among the dangerous habits.

facts.quote: Some of our human tendencies can be dangerous for investors.
facts.claim: The guide introduces that list as human tendencies that can be dangerous for investors.

facts.quote: The Cup with Handle is a bullish continuation pattern that marks a consolidation period followed by a breakout.
facts.claim: The cup with handle is a bullish continuation pattern: a consolidation, then a breakout.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped and resemble a bowl or rounding bottom. A V-shaped bottom would be considered too sharp of a reversal to qualify.
facts.claim: The cup should be a U-shaped bowl; a V-shaped bottom is too sharp to qualify.

facts.quote: After the high forms on the cup's right side, a pullback forms the handle.
facts.claim: The handle is the pullback after the cup's right side makes its high.

facts.quote: The handle represents the final consolidation/pullback before the big breakout and can retrace up to 1/3 of the cup's advance, but usually not more.
facts.claim: The handle is the last pullback before the breakout and usually gives back no more than a third of the cup's advance.

facts.quote: The projected advance after breakout can be estimated by measuring the distance from the right peak of the cup to the bottom of the cup.
facts.claim: The cup's target is its depth, right peak to bottom, projected from the breakout.

facts.quote: A rounded turn that looks like a cup with a handle on the right of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski describes the shape as a rounded turn like a cup, with a handle on the right.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped, but allow variations.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped.

facts.quote: Handle 1 week minimum with no maximum, forming in the upper half of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the handle lasts at least a week and forms in the upper half of the cup.

facts.quote: Cup rims should be near the same price level but be flexible.
facts.claim: The two rims of the cup should sit near the same price.

facts.quote: The handle low (point C ) is a good place to put a stop.
facts.claim: Bulkowski names the handle's low as a good place for the stop.

facts.quote: I looked at 300 cup with handle patterns, stretching from 1990 to March 2024.
facts.claim: Bulkowski studied 300 cup with handle patterns from 1990 to March 2024.

facts.quote: I found that 47% of the cup with handle patterns dropped substantially within two months of the breakout.
facts.claim: In that study, 47% dropped substantially within two months of the breakout.

facts.quote: If a trendline entry is not available, buy when price closes above the right cup rim
facts.claim: Bulkowski's basic entry is a close above the cup's right rim.

facts.quote: Pattern consists of a rounded bottom (not a “V” bottom), two “lips” at each end, and a “handle” (similar to a flag pattern) from the handle
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a rounded bottom, not a V, with a lip at each end and a handle.

facts.quote: Take the height of the right cup lip to the bottom of the cup, then add that amount to the breakout price.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: the cup target is the height from the right lip to the cup's bottom, added to the breakout price.

facts.quote: The buy point occurs when the stock breaks out or moves upward through the old point of resistance (right side of the cup).
facts.claim: Fidelity: the buy point is the breakout through the old resistance at the cup's right side.

facts.quote: The price target following the breakout can be estimated by measuring the distance from the right top of the cup to the bottom of the cup and adding that number to the buy point.
facts.claim: Fidelity: the cup target is the cup's depth added to the buy point.

facts.quote: This should be used only as a guideline.
facts.claim: Fidelity: use the cup's target only as a guideline.

facts.quote: This pattern typically forms over a period of seven to 65 weeks and is characterized by a "U" shaped cup followed by a downward sloping handle.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a U-shaped cup followed by a handle that slopes down.

facts.quote: Avoid handles that are overly deep also, as handles should form in the top half of the cup pattern.
facts.claim: Investopedia: avoid overly deep handles; the handle should form in the top half of the cup.

facts.quote: Place a stop buy order slightly above the upper trend line of the handle.
facts.claim: Investopedia's basic entry is a buy stop just above the handle's upper line.

facts.quote: You can place stop-loss orders below the handle or cup, based on your risk tolerance and market conditions.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the stop can go below the handle or below the cup.

facts.quote: The target with the cup and handle pattern is the height of the cup added to the breakout point of the handle.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the target is the cup's height added to the handle breakout.

facts.quote: A handle defines the proper entry. The highest price in the handle plus 10 cents
facts.claim: IBD: the handle sets the entry, at the handle's highest price plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: A flag is a small rectangle pattern that slopes against the previous trend.
facts.claim: A flag is a small rectangle sloping against the trend before it.

facts.quote: the price action needs to be contained within two parallel trend lines.
facts.claim: A flag's price action sits between two parallel lines.

facts.quote: A pennant is a small symmetrical triangle that begins wide and converges as the pattern matures (like a cone).
facts.claim: A pennant is a small symmetrical triangle whose lines converge.

facts.quote: The flagpole is the distance from the first resistance or support break to the high or low of the flag/pennant.
facts.claim: The flagpole is the sharp move leading into the flag or pennant.

facts.quote: Flags and pennants must be preceded by a sharp advance or decline.
facts.claim: Flags and pennants need a sharp advance or decline before them.

facts.quote: Once a flag is over 12 weeks old, it would be classified as a rectangle.
facts.claim: StockCharts reclassifies a flag older than 12 weeks as a rectangle.

facts.quote: volume expanded on the sharp advance to form the flagpole, contracted during the flag's formation, and expanded right after the resistance breakout.
facts.claim: Volume expands on the pole, contracts in the flag and expands again on the breakout.

facts.quote: The flagpole length can be applied to the resistance break or support break of the flag/pennant to estimate the advance or decline.
facts.claim: A flag or pennant target is the pole's length applied to the breakout.

facts.quote: Flag A continuation chart pattern that generally lasts less than three weeks and resembles a parallelogram that slopes against the prevailing trend.
facts.claim: StockCharts glossary: a flag is a short continuation pattern, a parallelogram sloping against the trend.

facts.quote: Flags appear as small rectangles usually tilted against the prevailing price trend and mounted at the end of a flagpole.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags are small rectangles tilted against the trend, hanging off a flagpole.

facts.quote: If you don't have a straight-line (or a quick move) price run (the flagpole), then you don't have a flag.
facts.claim: No quick, straight-line run (the flagpole), no flag.

facts.quote: Price moves between two parallel, or near parallel, trendlines.
facts.claim: In a flag, price moves between two parallel or near-parallel lines.

facts.quote: Flags are short, less than 3 weeks long. Patterns longer than that are rectangles or channels.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags last under three weeks; longer ones are rectangles or channels.

facts.quote: Prices move between two converging trendlines.
facts.claim: In a pennant, price moves between two converging lines.

facts.quote: Volume trend Downward trend 86% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski found pennant volume trending down 86% of the time.

facts.quote: Pennants are short, 3 weeks long or less. Patterns longer than that are symmetrical triangles
facts.claim: Pennants last three weeks or less; longer ones are symmetrical triangles.

facts.quote: In technical analysis, a flag is a price pattern that moves against the main trend in a shorter time frame, having the appearance of a flag on a flagpole.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a flag moves against the main trend and looks like a flag on a flagpole.

facts.quote: If lines converge, the patterns are referred to as a wedge or pennant pattern.
facts.claim: Investopedia: when the lines converge instead of running parallel, it's a wedge or pennant, not a flag.

facts.quote: In a typical flag pattern, volume will increase during the initial trend and then decrease or hold level during the consolidation period.
facts.claim: Investopedia: volume rises on the initial move and falls or holds level in the flag.

facts.quote: The initial move must be met with large volume, while the pennant should have weakening volume
facts.claim: Investopedia: heavy volume on the pole, weakening volume in the pennant.

facts.quote: The price target is often set by adding the flagpole’s height to the breakout point.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the pennant target adds the flagpole's height to the breakout point.

facts.quote: Pennants have converging trendlines that form a small symmetrical triangle.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a pennant's converging lines form a small symmetrical triangle.

facts.quote: These patterns are often preceded by a steep, sharp price change, up or down, and form a short consolidation that appears like a triangle or flag.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: flags and pennants follow a steep, sharp move and are short consolidations.

facts.quote: Bounded by two trend lines, each headed in the same direction; Price must touch a trend line at least five times (3 times on one and 2 times on the other) before a breakout
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a wedge's two lines point the same way, with at least five touches, three on one line and two on the other.

facts.quote: Performance in both types is below average, and retracements are very common
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: both wedge types perform below average.

facts.quote: Price bounces between two up-sloping and converging trendlines.
facts.claim: A rising wedge sits between two up-sloping lines that converge.

facts.quote: Price should touch (at a minor high or minor low) each trendline at least five times to outline a good pattern. That's 3 touches of one trendline and 2 of the opposite.
facts.claim: Bulkowski wants at least five touches: three on one line and two on the other.

facts.quote: Breakout Can be in any direction but is downward 60% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: rising wedges can break either way; downward 60% of the time.

facts.quote: Rising wedges, especially for downward breakouts, are some of the worst performing chart patterns.
facts.claim: Bulkowski calls rising wedges some of the worst-performing chart patterns.

facts.quote: The pattern confirms as a valid one when price closes outside one of the trendlines.
facts.claim: A wedge confirms only on a close outside one of its lines.

facts.quote: Price follows two down-sloping and converging trendlines.
facts.claim: A falling wedge sits between two down-sloping lines that converge.

facts.quote: The falling wedge is a poor performer as far as bullish chart patterns go.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the falling wedge is a poor performer among bullish patterns.

facts.quote: The Rising Wedge is a bearish pattern that begins wide at the bottom and contracts as prices move higher and the trading range narrows.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the rising wedge is bearish; it narrows as prices rise.

facts.quote: While it is a consolidation formation, the loss of upside momentum on each successive high gives the pattern its bearish bias.
facts.claim: Its bearish bias comes from upside momentum fading on each new high.

facts.quote: In contrast to symmetrical triangles , which have no definitive slope and no bullish or bearish bias, rising wedges definitely slope up and have a bearish bias.
facts.claim: Unlike the neutral symmetrical triangle, the rising wedge slopes up and carries a bearish bias.

facts.quote: The Falling Wedge is a bullish pattern that begins wide at the top and contracts as prices move lower.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the falling wedge is bullish; it narrows as prices fall.

facts.quote: The reaction lows penetrate the previous lows, but this penetration becomes shallower. Shallower lows indicate a decrease in selling pressure
facts.claim: In a falling wedge each new low is only a little lower, which shows selling pressure easing.

facts.quote: Usually, a rising wedge pattern is bearish
facts.claim: Investopedia: a rising wedge is usually bearish.

facts.quote: A falling wedge pattern is seen as a bullish signal
facts.claim: Investopedia: a falling wedge is seen as bullish.

facts.quote: Ascending Triangle A sideways price pattern between two converging trend lines in which the lower line is rising while the upper line is flat.
facts.claim: An ascending triangle has a flat upper line and a rising lower line.

facts.quote: Two trendlines bound prices; the top trendline is horizontal and the bottom one slopes upward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: ascending triangle, flat top line, rising bottom line.

facts.quote: Bounded by a horizontal upper trend line and an upward sloping lower trend line.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: ascending triangle, flat upper line, rising lower line.

facts.quote: It's these higher lows that indicate increased buying pressure and give the ascending triangle its bullish bias .
facts.claim: The rising lows show buyers stepping in higher, which gives the ascending triangle its bullish bias.

facts.quote: Breakout Upward 63% of the time and 64% of the way to the triangle apex (for both breakout directions).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: ascending triangles break upward 63% of the time.

facts.quote: Prices can break in either direction, but more commonly upward
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: an ascending triangle can break either way, more often up.

facts.quote: Descending Triangle A sideways price pattern between two converging trend lines in which the upper trend line is descending while the lower line is flat.
facts.claim: A descending triangle has a flat lower line and a falling upper line.

facts.quote: A price pattern bounded by two trendlines, the bottom one horizontal and the top sloping downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: descending triangle, flat bottom line, falling top line.

facts.quote: Bounded by two trend lines; the lower is horizontal and the upper slopes downward
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: descending triangle, flat lower line, falling upper line.

facts.quote: Breakout Can be in any direction but is upward 53% of the time.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: descending triangles break either way; upward 53% of the time.

facts.quote: Prices can break in either direction but most commonly downward
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a descending triangle can break either way, most commonly down.

facts.quote: Regardless of where they form, descending triangles are bearish patterns that indicate distribution.
facts.claim: StockCharts calls descending triangles bearish patterns.

facts.quote: It's because the pattern isn't complete until support is broken.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a descending triangle isn't complete until support breaks.

facts.quote: The pattern confirms as a valid one when price closes outside one of the trendlines.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a descending triangle confirms on a close outside one of its lines.

facts.quote: The symmetrical triangle, which can also be referred to as a coil, usually forms during a trend as a continuation pattern.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the symmetrical triangle is also called a coil.

facts.quote: Symmetrical triangles, sometimes called coils, appear often on the historical price chart but performance is awful.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: symmetrical triangles are sometimes called coils.

facts.quote: A symmetrical triangle pattern, also known as a coil, appears on trading charts when two converging trend lines connect sequential peaks and troughs.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a symmetrical triangle is also known as a coil.

facts.quote: Symmetrical Triangle A sideways chart pattern between two converging trend lines in which the upper trend line is declining and the lower trend line is rising.
facts.claim: A symmetrical triangle has a falling upper line and a rising lower line that converge.

facts.quote: Two trendlines bound prices; the bottom trendline slopes up and the top one slopes down.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: symmetrical triangle, bottom line up, top line down.

facts.quote: Bounded by a downward sloping upper trend line and an upward sloping lower trend line.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: symmetrical triangle, falling upper line, rising lower line.

facts.quote: The ideal breakout point occurs 1/2 to 3/4 of the pattern's development or time span, which can be measured from the apex (convergence of upper and lower lines) back to the beginning of the lower trend line (base).
facts.claim: The apex is where the two lines converge; the ideal breakout comes one-half to three-quarters of the way to it.

facts.quote: A break before the 1/2 way point might be premature, and a break too close to the apex may be insignificant.
facts.claim: A break before halfway may be premature; one too close to the apex may mean little.

facts.quote: Breakout Upward 60% of the time and 74% of the way to the triangle apex (for both breakout directions).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: symmetrical triangles break out about 74% of the way to the apex.

facts.quote: The average distance from the breakout is 61% to 62% of the way to the triangle apex (where the trendlines join).
facts.claim: Bulkowski defines the apex as where the trendlines join.

facts.quote: Price trend Can be any direction leading to the chart pattern.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the trend into a symmetrical triangle can be either direction.

facts.quote: flags and pennants require a sudden shift before they form. Symmetrical triangles can take shape without such a prior movement.
facts.claim: Investopedia: pennants need a sudden prior move; symmetrical triangles don't.

facts.quote: The pattern is usually considered a pennant if it is less than three weeks.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a symmetrical triangle under three weeks is usually called a pennant.

facts.quote: The pattern forms with two consecutive troughs that are roughly equal, a moderate peak in between and a resistance breakout.
facts.claim: A double bottom is two roughly equal troughs with a moderate peak between, then a breakout.

facts.quote: Breaking resistance from the highest point between the troughs completes the Double Bottom Reversal.
facts.claim: A double bottom completes when price breaks above the high between the two lows.

facts.quote: typically, a trough within 3% of its predecessor is considered valid.
facts.claim: StockCharts accepts a second low within 3% of the first.

facts.quote: Two successive troughs separated by a peak
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a double bottom is two troughs separated by a peak.

facts.quote: Price must break out of middle peak
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: price must break out above the middle peak.

facts.quote: This pattern resembles the letter “W” and involves a security or index experiencing two distinct lows at approximately the same level, with rebounds in between.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a double bottom looks like a W, two lows at about the same level.

facts.quote: A long position is recommended on a daily close above the first rebound’s high, with a stop loss at the pattern’s second low.
facts.claim: Investopedia: enter on a daily close above the middle high.

facts.quote: No, there is room to play with the relative levels of the lows, though they should be within 3% to 4% of each other.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the two lows should be within 3% to 4% of each other.

facts.quote: The pattern forms with two prominent peaks that are roughly equal, a moderate trough in-between and a support break.
facts.claim: A double top is two roughly equal peaks, a moderate trough between, then a support break.

facts.quote: Breaking support from the lowest point between the peaks completes the Double Top Reversal.
facts.claim: A double top completes on a break below the low between the peaks.

facts.quote: Perhaps the most important aspect of a Double Top Reversal is to avoid jumping the gun. Wait for support to be broken with an expansion of volume.
facts.claim: Don't jump the gun on a double top; wait for support to break.

facts.quote: Usually, a peak within 3% of the previous high is adequate.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a second peak within 3% of the first is close enough.

facts.quote: Price must break out of middle reversal point
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a double top needs a break of the middle low.

facts.quote: A double top pattern forms when a strong uptrend is followed by two distinct peaks at roughly the same price level with a trough in between.
facts.claim: Schwab: a double top is two peaks at about the same price with a trough between.

facts.quote: There are three equal highs followed by a break below support .
facts.claim: A triple top is three equal highs, then a break below support.

facts.quote: Three distinct peaks at roughly the same price level separated by two intermittent troughs
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a triple top is three peaks at about the same price with two troughs between.

facts.quote: Of these patterns mentioned, only the ascending triangle has bullish overtones; the others are neutral until a break occurs.
facts.claim: Three equal highs can also be part of an ascending triangle, which carries a bullish bias.

facts.quote: Three distinct troughs at roughly the same price level separated by two intermittent peaks at any level
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a triple bottom is three lows at about the same price.

facts.quote: Head and Shoulders Top A bearish reversal pattern marked by three (or more) prominent peaks with a middle peak (the head) that is higher than the other peaks (the shoulders).
facts.claim: A head and shoulders top has a middle peak, the head, higher than the shoulders either side.

facts.quote: The pattern contains three successive peaks, with the middle peak ( head ) being the highest and the two outside peaks ( shoulders ) being low and roughly equal.
facts.claim: Three peaks: the middle one highest, the outer two lower and roughly equal.

facts.quote: The reaction lows of each peak can be connected to form support or a neckline
facts.claim: The neckline connects the lows between the peaks.

facts.quote: The head and shoulders pattern isn't complete, and the uptrend is not reversed until the neckline support is broken.
facts.claim: A head and shoulders isn't complete until the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: This distance is then subtracted from the neckline to reach a price target.
facts.claim: The head-to-neckline distance is subtracted from the neckline for the target.

facts.quote: After breaking neckline support, the projected price decline is found by measuring the distance from the neckline to the top of the head.
facts.claim: The projected decline is the distance from the neckline to the top of the head.

facts.quote: Without a prior uptrend to reverse, there cannot be a Head and Shoulders reversal pattern
facts.claim: No prior uptrend, no head and shoulders top.

facts.quote: Neckline In a head-and-shoulders chart pattern, a line joining the armpits, extended into the future to show trading signals when price crosses it.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the neckline joins the armpits, the low points between the peaks.

facts.quote: A three-peak pattern with the middle peak above the others.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: three peaks, the middle one above the others.

facts.quote: Price must have something to reverse, so if the rise leading to the pattern is small, expect a small decline.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a reversal needs something to reverse.

facts.quote: Three peaks with center peak higher than the other two
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: three peaks, the center one highest.

facts.quote: Pattern is only complete on breaking the neckline
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: the pattern is complete only when the neckline breaks.

facts.quote: Target is the distance from the head to the neckline projected from the neckline
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: target is the head-to-neckline distance projected from the neckline.

facts.quote: is formed by drawing a line underneath the troughs established just before and just after the head.
facts.claim: Schwab: the neckline is drawn under the troughs just before and after the head.

facts.quote: Indeed, many investors have paid a steep price for placing a trade without waiting for signals confirming the pattern.
facts.claim: Schwab: many investors have paid for trading the pattern before it confirmed.

facts.quote: Trend reversals require strong trends leading into them.
facts.claim: Schwab: a reversal needs a strong trend leading into it.

facts.quote: In my experience, those new to technical analysis tend to see head-and-shoulders patterns everywhere.
facts.claim: Schwab: newcomers tend to see head and shoulders patterns everywhere.

facts.quote: The pattern contains three successive troughs with the middle trough (head) being the deepest and the two outside troughs (shoulders) being shallower.
facts.claim: A head and shoulders bottom has three troughs, the middle one deepest.

facts.quote: An inverse head and shoulders pattern, often called a head and shoulders bottom, suggests a reversal from a bearish to a bullish trend, formed by three troughs.
facts.claim: Investopedia: the inverse head and shoulders, or head and shoulders bottom, is formed by three troughs.

facts.quote: A 3-valley pattern with the middle valley below the others.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a head and shoulders bottom is three valleys, the middle one lowest.

facts.quote: Confirmation Wait for confirmation before placing a trade.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: wait for confirmation before trading it.

facts.quote: The pattern confirms as a valid one when price closes above a down-sloping neckline
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a head and shoulders bottom confirms on a close above the neckline.

facts.quote: When the trend line (neckline) connecting the peaks at the top of the pattern is broken, the pattern is complete.
facts.claim: StockCharts: the bottom version completes when its neckline breaks.

facts.quote: The Rounding Bottom is a long-term reversal pattern best suited for weekly charts. It is also referred to as a saucer bottom.
facts.claim: A rounding bottom, also called a saucer bottom, is a long-term pattern best seen on weekly charts.

facts.quote: Rounding bottoms are chart patterns that are difficult to spot unless you look on the weekly scale.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: rounding bottoms are hard to spot except on the weekly scale.

facts.claim: Bulkowski: a rounded bowl, usually over many months.
