facts.claim: Bulkowski uses the word saucer for the rounding bottom's rim.

facts.quote: Rounding Bottom Also known as a saucer bottom, it is a reversal chart pattern representing a long consolidation period that turns from a bearish bias to a bullish bias.
facts.claim: StockCharts glossary: a rounding bottom is also known as a saucer bottom.

facts.quote: Rectangle A continuation chart pattern where prices move sideways between two different levels for a period of time and then continue moving in the direction of the previous trend.
facts.claim: A rectangle is price moving sideways between two levels.

facts.quote: Rectangles are sometimes referred to as trading ranges, consolidation zones, or congestion areas.
facts.claim: Rectangles are also called trading ranges or congestion areas.

facts.quote: Prices have flat tops and flat bottoms, crossing the pattern from side to side following two parallel trendlines.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a rectangle has flat tops and flat bottoms between two parallel lines.

facts.quote: Trading range with support and resistance levels bounding price action
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a rectangle is a trading range bounded by support and resistance.

facts.quote: If you know what a rectangle chart pattern looks like, then you know what a flat base is. Look for a price area in which the stock touches the same value multiple times over several weeks or months.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a flat base looks like a rectangle, price touching the same levels over several weeks or months.

facts.quote: Look for price moving horizontally.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: in a flat base, price moves horizontally.

facts.quote: Rather than go on an uptrend or downtrend, the stock moves sideways
facts.claim: IBD: in a flat base the stock moves sideways, neither up nor down.

facts.quote: It places a stock’s price within a “box” based on recent highs and lows, then signals a buying opportunity when the price breaks above the box on strong volume.
facts.claim: Investopedia: a Darvas box frames price by recent highs and lows; a break above it is the buy signal.

facts.quote: You find a Darvas box and wait for price to close outside the box's boundaries.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: find the box and wait for a close outside it.

facts.quote: Find the top of the box, which is the highest high for the next three days (4 days total).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the box top is a high that holds for the next three days.

facts.quote: Spring A situation that occurs when prices break below support but soon reverse course and move back above support.
facts.claim: A spring is a break below support that soon reverses back above it.

facts.quote: A “spring” takes price below the low of the TR and then reverses to close within the TR
facts.claim: In Wyckoff's terms a spring dips below the trading range's low and closes back inside the range.

facts.quote: Spring : Price thrusts sharply below a trading range/prior low support level (often in reaction to bearish news) before quickly reversing and closing back above the violated support.
facts.claim: CMT Association: a spring thrusts below a range's support, then quickly closes back above it.

facts.quote: Upthrust : Price thrusts sharply above the trading range/prior resistance level (often in reaction to bullish news) before quickly reversing and closing below the violated resistance.
facts.claim: CMT Association: an upthrust pushes above a range's resistance, then quickly closes back below it.

facts.quote: It is a price move above TR resistance that quickly reverses and closes in the TR.
facts.claim: Wyckoff's upthrust is a move above the range's resistance that quickly closes back inside.

facts.quote: However, springs and terminal shakeouts are not required elements
facts.claim: Springs and terminal shakeouts are not required in a Wyckoff accumulation range.

facts.quote: However, springs and terminal shakeouts are not required elements
facts.claim: Wyckoff Analytics: springs and terminal shakeouts are not required.

facts.quote: Accumulation Schematic 1 depicts a spring, while Accumulation Schematic 2 shows a TR without a spring.
facts.claim: One Wyckoff accumulation schematic has a spring; the other has none.

facts.quote: Shakeouts may also occur once a price advance has started, with rapid downward movement intended to induce retail traders and investors in long positions to sell their shares to large operators.
facts.claim: A shakeout is a rapid drop that pushes holders to sell, and it can come once an advance has started.

facts.quote: Shakeout A situation where many scared investors exit their positions due to unfavorable news or uncertainty regarding the stock or industry.
facts.claim: StockCharts glossary: a shakeout is many scared investors exiting at once.

facts.quote: A shakeout is a situation in which many investors exit their positions in a stock or market segment at the same time, often at a loss.
facts.claim: Investopedia: in a shakeout many investors exit at the same time, often at a loss.

facts.quote: Shakeouts can be quite variable in duration, but they’re usually sharp in terms of the amount lost from recent highs.
facts.claim: Investopedia: shakeouts are usually sharp drops from recent highs.

facts.quote: a shakeout is almost exclusively used to refer to an interruption in a longer-term bullish trend.
facts.claim: Investopedia: in technical analysis, a shakeout means an interruption in a longer-term uptrend.

facts.quote: After the shakeout, the previous trend often reasserts.
facts.claim: Investopedia: after a shakeout the prior trend often reasserts.

facts.quote: The law of cause and effect helps the trader and investor set price objectives by gauging the potential extent of a trend emerging from a trading range.
facts.claim: Wyckoff's law of cause and effect gauges how far a trend coming out of a trading range may go.

facts.quote: In Wyckoffian analysis, Phase B serves the function of “building a cause” for a new uptrend
facts.claim: In Wyckoff's accumulation range, Phase B builds the cause for the next uptrend.

facts.quote: Wyckoff's “cause” can be measured by the horizontal point count in a Point-and-Figure chart, while the “effect” is the distance price moves corresponding to the point count.
facts.claim: Wyckoff Analytics: the cause is built in the range (measured by a point count); the effect is the move that follows.

facts.quote: Busted patterns Price that moves no more than 10% after the breakout before reversing and zipping to the other side of the chart pattern, starting a trend in a new direction.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a busted pattern moves no more than 10% after the breakout, then reverses through the other side.

facts.quote: When price rises less than 10%, reverses, and closes below the bottom of the chart pattern (not below the trendline), it's said to have busted the upward breakout.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: rising less than 10% then closing below the pattern's bottom busts the upward breakout.

facts.quote: Failed Breakout (Trap) False breakout occurs and the price then breaks out in the opposite direction.
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a failed breakout, or trap, is a false breakout followed by a break the other way.

facts.quote: Throwbacks Price breaks out upward, climbs, and then returns to the breakout price within 30 days.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a throwback is a return to the breakout price after an upward breakout.

facts.quote: False breakouts, bogus reads, and exceptions to the rule are all part of the ongoing education.
facts.claim: StockCharts: false breakouts and exceptions come with pattern reading.

facts.quote: Targets are only meant to be used as guidelines, and other aspects of technical analysis should also be employed for deciding when to sell.
facts.claim: StockCharts: pattern targets are guidelines only.

facts.quote: Three equal lows followed by a break above resistance.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a triple bottom is three equal lows, then a break above resistance.

facts.quote: Flags and Pennants are short-term continuation patterns that mark a small consolidation before the previous move resumes.
facts.claim: Flags and pennants are short continuation patterns: a small pause, then the prior move resumes.

facts.quote: The cup forms after an advance and looks like a bowl or rounding bottom.
facts.claim: Fidelity: the cup forms after an advance and looks like a bowl.

facts.quote: The softer “U” shape ensures that the cup is a consolidation pattern with valid support at the bottom of the “U.”
facts.claim: The rounded U shows a real consolidation with support at its bottom.

facts.quote: the horizontal line represents overhead supply that prevents the security from moving past a certain level.
facts.claim: In an ascending triangle the flat top is supply capping price at one level.

facts.quote: The extent of accumulation or distribution determines the cause that unfolds in the subsequent move out of the TR.
facts.claim: The accumulation or distribution inside the range is the cause that plays out in the move out of it.

facts.quote: Raise the stop as price rises.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: raise the stop as price rises.

facts.quote: However, most chart patterns fall into two main groups
facts.claim: Most chart patterns fall into two main groups, reversals and continuations.

facts.quote: Reversal patterns indicate a trend change and can be broken down into top and bottom formations.
facts.claim: Reversal patterns signal a trend change and split into tops and bottoms.

facts.quote: Measure the height from the right cup lip (A) to the lowest valley (B)
facts.claim: Bulkowski also calls the cup's top edges its lips; his target measures down from the right cup lip.

facts.quote: The pattern confirms as a valid one when price closes below an up-sloping neckline or below the right armpit when the neckline slopes downward.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a head and shoulders top confirms on a close below the neckline (below the right armpit when the neckline slopes down).

facts.quote: Pattern is complete with breakout above both lips. Often have a throwback
facts.claim: Fidelity's guide: a cup with handle completes on a breakout above both lips, and these often throw back afterward.

facts.quote: Trader analyst measures the cause built up during a trading range on P&F chart and then projects a price objective representing the potential effect of it.
facts.claim: Pruden (CMT Association): the cause is built up during a trading range, and the projected move out of it is its effect.

walkthroughs.title: A pause or a turn
steps: Most chart patterns fall into two groups. A continuation is a pause, and the old trend resumes after it.
A reversal forms before the trend turns the other way. Tops and bottoms live here.
Either way, a pattern isn't complete until price breaks out of it. Until then it's just a shape.

walkthroughs.title: The cup and its handle
steps: The cup is a U-shaped bowl that forms after an advance. A sharp V doesn't count.
The handle is the short pullback off the cup's right side. It should stay in the upper half of the cup.
The classic entry is a break above the top of the handle. The handle's low is a natural place for the stop.

walkthroughs.title: Lines that frame the pause
steps: A flag hangs off a sharp run, the flagpole. Its two lines run parallel and tilt against the run.
A pennant is the same idea, but its lines come together like a tiny triangle.
Triangles and wedges have converging lines too. The point where the lines meet is the apex.
In a wedge both lines slope the same way. In a triangle they don't.

questions.q: What does continuation pattern mean?
choices: A pause, then the trend resumes
A sign the trend is about to flip
Any pattern that breaks out upward
questions.answer: A pause, then the trend resumes
questions.why: A pause, then the old trend resumes. Price goes into the pattern one way and comes out the same way.
questions.lesson_line: Continuation: in one direction, out the same direction.

wrong.A sign the trend is about to flip: That's a reversal pattern. The trend changes direction after it.
wrong.Any pattern that breaks out upward: Direction isn't the test. A continuation inside a downtrend breaks out lower.

questions.q: Which word is this: a chart pattern that forms before the trend changes direction.
choices: Reversal pattern
Continuation pattern
Flag
Pennant
questions.why: Reversal pattern. Price enters it going one way and leaves going the other.
questions.lesson_line: Reversal: in one way, out the other.

wrong.Continuation pattern: A continuation is a pause. The old trend resumes after it.
wrong.Flag: A flag is a continuation pattern: a short pause, then the prior move resumes.
wrong.Pennant: A pennant is a continuation pattern too: a short pause before the prior move resumes.

questions.q: What does cup with handle mean?
choices: U-shaped base plus a short pullback
Three peaks, the middle one highest
Two equal lows shaped like a W
A sharp V-shaped drop and rebound
questions.answer: U-shaped base plus a short pullback
questions.why: A U-shaped base plus a short pullback. The cup is a rounded bowl after an advance; the handle is the dip off its right side.
questions.lesson_line: Cup first, handle second, breakout third.

wrong.A sharp V-shaped drop and rebound: A V is too sharp to count. The cup should be a U.

questions.q: On a cup with handle, what is the handle?
choices: The short pullback after the cup
The deepest low of the whole cup
The run-up before the cup began
The day price breaks out of it
questions.answer: The short pullback after the cup
questions.why: The short pullback after the cup. Once the cup's right side makes its high, price eases back for a while. That dip is the handle.
questions.lesson_line: The handle is the last pause before the breakout.

wrong.The deepest low of the whole cup: That's the bottom of the cup.
wrong.The run-up before the cup began: That's the prior advance. The pattern needs one, but it isn't the handle.
wrong.The day price breaks out of it: The breakout comes out of the handle. It isn't the handle.

questions.q: A sharp V-shaped bottom is the ideal shape for the cup.
questions.why: False. The cup should be a U, a rounded bowl. A V is too sharp a reversal to qualify.
questions.lesson_line: U, not V. The rounded bottom is where support gets built.

questions.q: What does flag mean on a chart?
choices: Brief pause tilting against the move
A long base shaped like a round bowl
Lines that meet at a point
The sharp run that comes before it
questions.answer: Brief pause tilting against the move
questions.why: A brief pause tilting against the move. It's a small rectangle hanging off a sharp run, usually sloping the other way.
questions.lesson_line: A flag leans against the move it interrupts.

wrong.A long base shaped like a round bowl: That's a rounding bottom, or the cup of a cup with handle.
wrong.Lines that meet at a point: Converging lines make a pennant or a triangle. A flag's lines run parallel.
wrong.The sharp run that comes before it: That's the flagpole. The flag is the pause that hangs off it.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The sharp, near-straight run that comes before a flag is the ___.
questions.why: Flagpole. No sharp run, no flag. The pole is what the flag hangs off.
questions.lesson_line: No pole, no flag.

questions.q: What does pennant mean?
choices: A tiny triangle after a sharp move
A long, flat-topped base of weeks
A flag-like pause with parallel lines
A deep U-shaped base with a handle
questions.answer: A tiny triangle after a sharp move
questions.why: A tiny triangle after a sharp move. It's a short pause between two lines that come together.
questions.lesson_line: Pennant: a small triangle on a flagpole.

wrong.A long, flat-topped base of weeks: That sounds like an ascending triangle or a flat base. A pennant is short and its lines converge.
wrong.A flag-like pause with parallel lines: Parallel lines make a flag. A pennant's lines come together.

questions.q: A flag's two lines run parallel. A pennant's two lines come together.
questions.why: True. That's the difference. Both hang off a sharp run and both are short pauses.
questions.lesson_line: Parallel lines: flag. Converging lines: pennant.

questions.q: What does wedge mean on a chart?
choices: Narrowing lines sloping the same way
One flat line and one rising line
Parallel lines tilting against a run
A rounded low with a short dip
questions.answer: Narrowing lines sloping the same way
questions.why: Narrowing lines that slope the same way. Both lines rise in a rising wedge; both fall in a falling wedge.
questions.lesson_line: Wedge: both lines point the same way and squeeze together.

wrong.One flat line and one rising line: That's an ascending triangle. In a wedge neither line is flat.

questions.q: Which word is this: a flat top line and a rising bottom line that close in on each other.
choices: Ascending triangle
Descending triangle
Symmetrical triangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: Ascending triangle. Sellers cap price at the same level while buyers step in at higher and higher lows.
questions.lesson_line: Flat top, rising lows: ascending triangle.

wrong.Descending triangle: That's the mirror image: a flat bottom with falling highs.
wrong.Symmetrical triangle: In a symmetrical triangle neither line is flat.
wrong.Rising wedge: In a rising wedge both lines slope up.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A flat bottom line with lower and lower highs above it is a ___ triangle.
questions.why: Descending. The floor stays flat while each rally tops out lower.
questions.lesson_line: Flat floor, falling highs: descending triangle.

questions.q: Which pattern do some chart books also call a coil?
choices: Symmetrical triangle
Head and shoulders
Double bottom
Rounding bottom
questions.why: The symmetrical triangle. Lower highs and higher lows squeeze price into a narrower and narrower range.
questions.lesson_line: Coil is another name for the symmetrical triangle.

wrong.Head and shoulders: Three peaks with the middle one highest. Nothing narrows to a point.
wrong.Double bottom: Two lows with a peak between. The range doesn't narrow.
wrong.Rounding bottom: That's the slow bowl, also called a saucer.

questions.q: On a triangle, what is the apex?
choices: Where the two lines meet
The widest part of the pattern
The breakout day's high
The first low in the pattern
questions.why: Where the two lines meet. Extend the top and bottom lines forward and the apex is the point where they join.
questions.lesson_line: The apex is where a triangle's lines meet.

wrong.The widest part of the pattern: The widest part is the start of the triangle, the opposite end from the apex.
wrong.The breakout day's high: The breakout is where price leaves the pattern, usually before it reaches the apex.
wrong.The first low in the pattern: That's just the first touch of the lower line.

questions.q: What does double bottom mean?
choices: Two similar lows with a peak between
Two similar highs with a dip between
Three lows, the middle one deepest
A slow, rounded low over months
questions.answer: Two similar lows with a peak between
questions.why: Two similar lows with a peak between. It looks like a W.
questions.lesson_line: Double bottom: a W, two lows near the same price.

wrong.Three lows, the middle one deepest: That's an inverse head and shoulders.
wrong.A slow, rounded low over months: That's a rounding bottom, or saucer.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Two roughly equal peaks with a dip between them form a ___ top.
questions.why: Double. Two peaks near the same price, a moderate trough between, then a break below that trough.
questions.lesson_line: Double top: two peaks, and it isn't done until the low between them breaks.

questions.q: Which word is this: three peaks, the middle one highest, the outer two about level.
choices: Head and shoulders
Triple top
Double top
Rising wedge
questions.why: Head and shoulders. The middle peak is the head; the lower peaks either side are the shoulders.
questions.lesson_line: Head above, shoulders level on either side.

wrong.Triple top: A triple top has three peaks at about the same price.
wrong.Rising wedge: That's two rising lines squeezing together, with no head.

questions.q: In a head and shoulders top, what is the neckline?
choices: Line through the lows between peaks
Line across the two shoulder tops
The highest point of the head
The uptrend line under the whole move
questions.answer: Line through the lows between peaks
questions.why: The line through the lows between the peaks. Join the dip after the left shoulder to the dip after the head.
questions.lesson_line: The neckline is the floor of the top. The break of it decides the pattern.

wrong.Line across the two shoulder tops: That line sits above the pattern's lows. The neckline runs through the lows.
wrong.The highest point of the head: That's the head's peak. It's used to measure the target, not to draw the neckline.
wrong.The uptrend line under the whole move: That's a trend line. The neckline is drawn through the pattern's own lows.

questions.q: What does inverse head and shoulders mean?
choices: Three lows, the middle one deepest
Three peaks, the middle one highest
Two equal lows with a peak between
Three equal lows in a row
questions.answer: Three lows, the middle one deepest
questions.why: Three lows, the middle one deepest. It's a head and shoulders turned upside down, also called a head and shoulders bottom.
questions.lesson_line: Flip a head and shoulders top and you get the bottom version.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A rounding bottom is also called a ___ bottom.
questions.why: Saucer. It's a slow, bowl-shaped turn, easiest to see on a weekly chart.
questions.lesson_line: Rounding bottom and saucer: same slow bowl.

questions.q: What does rectangle mean on a chart?
choices: Sideways between flat top and bottom
A narrowing range that slopes upward
A U-shaped dip and slow recovery
Three peaks, the middle highest
questions.answer: Sideways between flat top and bottom
questions.why: Sideways between a flat top and a flat bottom. It's also called a trading range or a congestion area.
questions.lesson_line: Rectangle: flat ceiling, flat floor, price bouncing between.

questions.q: A chart pattern is confirmed as soon as its shape looks finished, before any breakout.
questions.why: False. A pattern isn't complete until price breaks out of it. Before that it's squiggles that might become a pattern.
questions.lesson_line: No breakout, no pattern. The shape alone confirms nothing.

questions.story: A stock runs from $40 to $60 in two months. It then moves sideways in a tight range for three weeks. Next it breaks out above the range.
questions.q: Which kind of pattern was the sideways range?
choices: Continuation pattern
Reversal pattern
Topping pattern
questions.why: A continuation pattern. Price came in going up and left going up. The range was a pause, not a turn.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a pattern by how price enters and leaves it.

wrong.Reversal pattern: A reversal leaves in the opposite direction. This one kept going up.
wrong.Topping pattern: A top ends an uptrend. This range led to higher prices.

questions.q: A pattern that forms after a big advance is automatically a reversal pattern.
questions.why: False. Many patterns after a big run are only pauses. A rectangle or a wedge can be either kind.
questions.lesson_line: Where a pattern forms doesn't decide its type. How price leaves it does.

questions.q: Cup low $40. Right lip and breakout $50. Add the cup's depth to the breakout: what's the textbook target?
questions.why: $60. The cup's depth, $50 less $40, added to the $50 breakout. It's a rough guide, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: Cup target: the cup's depth added to the breakout. A guide, not a promise.

questions.story: A stock builds a cup from $50 down to $35 and back up to $49. Then it pulls back to $38 over two weeks.
questions.q: Does that pullback count as a proper handle?
choices: No, it sank into the lower half
Yes, any dip after a cup counts
Yes, a deep handle shakes out more
No, a handle can only go sideways
questions.answer: No, it sank into the lower half
questions.why: No. The cup runs from $35 to $49, so $38 is deep in its lower half. A handle should stay in the upper half.
questions.lesson_line: A handle that sinks into the bottom of the cup isn't a handle.

wrong.Yes, any dip after a cup counts: Where the dip ends matters. The handle should stay in the cup's upper half.
wrong.Yes, a deep handle shakes out more: Depth isn't a virtue here. Overly deep handles are the ones to avoid.
wrong.No, a handle can only go sideways: Handles can drift lower. The problem is how deep this one went.

questions.q: On a cup with handle, where is the classic buy point?
choices: Just above the top of the handle
At the lowest point of the cup
Halfway down the handle
At the first up day in the cup
questions.answer: Just above the top of the handle
questions.why: Just above the top of the handle. IBD puts it at the handle's highest price plus 10 cents; Fidelity at the break through the cup's right side.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the break out of the handle, not a guess inside the pattern.

wrong.At the lowest point of the cup: That's buying a falling stock before any pattern exists.
wrong.Halfway down the handle: That's a guess inside the pattern, before it breaks out.
wrong.At the first up day in the cup: Far too early. The cup isn't finished and there's no handle yet.

questions.q: On a cup with handle, what is a lip?
choices: A high at the cup's top edge
The lowest point of the cup
The low of the handle
The breakout day's close
questions.answer: A high at the cup's top edge
questions.why: A high at the cup's top edge. There's one on each side, and the handle forms after the right one.
questions.lesson_line: Two lips, one each side of the cup, near the same price.

wrong.The low of the handle: That's the handle's low, a common place for the stop.
wrong.The breakout day's close: That's the breakout. The lips come before it.

questions.q: The flagpole runs from $20 to $30. The flag breaks out at $28. Add the pole's length to the breakout: what's the target?
questions.why: $38. The pole's length, $30 less $20, added to the $28 breakout. It's an estimate, nothing more.
questions.lesson_line: Flag target: the pole's length added to the breakout.

questions.story: A stock jumps 25% in six sessions on heavy volume. It then drifts lower for eight days between two parallel lines. Volume shrinks.
questions.q: Which word fits the drift?
choices: Flag
Pennant
Rounding bottom
Double top
questions.why: Flag. The sharp run is the pole; the short drift between parallel lines, on lighter volume, is the flag.
questions.lesson_line: Pole, then a short parallel drift on light volume: that's a flag.

wrong.Pennant: A pennant's lines converge. These run parallel.
wrong.Rounding bottom: That's a slow bowl over many months, not a drift of a few days.
wrong.Double top: That needs two peaks near the same price. This is one run and a drift.

questions.q: A flag that keeps drifting for four months is still called a flag.
questions.why: False. Flags are short pauses. Bulkowski calls longer ones rectangles or channels; StockCharts calls a flag over 12 weeks old a rectangle.
questions.lesson_line: A long flag stops being a flag. Call it what it has become.

questions.q: Volume usually shrinks while a pennant forms.
questions.why: True. Volume is heavy on the pole and fades in the pennant. Bulkowski found it trending down 86% of the time.
questions.lesson_line: Loud pole, quiet pennant. Watch for volume to return on the break.

questions.q: At least how many touches, across both lines, do Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide want before calling it a wedge?
questions.why: 5. Three touches of one line and two of the other.
questions.lesson_line: Count the touches: three on one line, two on the other, before you call it a wedge.

questions.q: What bias do textbooks give the rising wedge?
choices: Bearish, though prices are rising
Bullish, because prices are rising
Neutral until it reaches the apex
questions.why: Bearish. Each push higher loses momentum, and the textbook reads that fading as a warning.
questions.lesson_line: Rising wedge: higher prices, weaker pushes. Textbooks lean bearish.

wrong.Bullish, because prices are rising: Rising prices are the trap. The squeeze shows upside momentum fading.
wrong.Neutral until it reaches the apex: No bias is the symmetrical triangle's reading. The rising wedge carries a bearish one.

questions.q: A rising wedge does not always break down; Bulkowski counts downward breakouts 60% of the time.
questions.why: True. Textbooks lean bearish, but Bulkowski counts downward breakouts 60% of the time, not every time.
questions.lesson_line: A bias is not a forecast. Wait for a close outside one of the lines.

questions.story: A stock slides for four months. Its lower highs and lower lows trace two falling lines that squeeze together. Each new low is only a bit lower.
questions.q: Which word fits?
choices: Falling wedge
Descending triangle
Bear flag
Rising wedge
questions.why: Falling wedge. Both lines slope down and converge, and the shallower lows show selling pressure easing.
questions.lesson_line: Both lines falling and squeezing together: falling wedge. Textbooks lean bullish.

wrong.Descending triangle: That needs a flat bottom line. Here the lows keep falling.
wrong.Bear flag: A flag's lines run parallel, and it's a short pause, not four months.

questions.story: Over three months a stock makes lower highs and higher lows. The upper line slopes down, the lower line slopes up, and they're closing in.
questions.q: Which word fits?
choices: Symmetrical triangle
Ascending triangle
Rectangle
Rising wedge
questions.why: Symmetrical triangle. One line falls, the other rises, and they converge. Neither line is flat.
questions.lesson_line: Lower highs plus higher lows, closing in: symmetrical triangle.

wrong.Ascending triangle: That needs a flat top line.
wrong.Rectangle: A rectangle's lines are flat and parallel. They never meet.
wrong.Rising wedge: In a wedge both lines slope the same way.

questions.q: In a symmetrical triangle, where does the ideal breakout come?
choices: Half to three-quarters of the way in
Right at the apex, where lines meet
In the first few days of the pattern
Only after price passes the apex
questions.answer: Half to three-quarters of the way in
questions.why: Half to three-quarters of the way in. StockCharts says a break too close to the apex may mean little. Bulkowski's symmetrical triangles break about 74% of the way to the apex.
questions.lesson_line: Good triangle breaks come before the apex, not at it.

wrong.Right at the apex, where lines meet: A break that close to the apex may be insignificant.
wrong.In the first few days of the pattern: Too early. A break before the halfway point may be premature.
wrong.Only after price passes the apex: Past the apex the lines have met. There's no pattern left to break.

questions.q: When is a double bottom complete?
choices: On a break above the middle peak
When the second low holds a day
When the second low matches the first
When volume spikes at the second low
questions.answer: On a break above the middle peak
questions.why: On a break above the middle peak. Until then you have two lows, not a finished pattern.
questions.lesson_line: A W isn't done until price clears the middle of the W.

wrong.When the second low holds a day: Holding is a start. The middle peak still has to break.
wrong.When the second low matches the first: Matching lows make it possible. They don't complete it.
wrong.When volume spikes at the second low: Volume can back up a breakout, but the break above the middle peak completes it.

questions.q: First low $50.00, second low $49.00. How far below the first low is the second, in percent?
questions.why: 2%. That's within the 3% StockCharts allows, so the two lows count as roughly equal.
questions.lesson_line: Two lows within about 3% of each other still count as roughly equal.

questions.story: A stock peaks at $80, dips to $70, then rallies to $79.50 and turns down. It now sits at $72.
questions.q: Is the double top complete?
choices: Not yet, it must break below $70
Yes, the second peak failed
Yes, two peaks at about one price
No, the peaks must match exactly
questions.answer: Not yet, it must break below $70
questions.why: Not yet. A double top completes on a break of the low between the peaks, here $70.
questions.lesson_line: Don't jump the gun on a double top. Wait for the middle low to break.

wrong.Yes, the second peak failed: A failed second peak sets it up. It doesn't complete it.
wrong.Yes, two peaks at about one price: Two peaks make it possible. The break of support completes it.
wrong.No, the peaks must match exactly: Exact peaks aren't needed. A second peak within 3% of the first is close enough.

questions.story: A stock makes three peaks: $48, $55, then $48.50. The dips between them both bottomed near $44. Price now sits at $45.
questions.q: What completes the head and shoulders top?
choices: A close under the $44 neckline
A new high above $55
A third peak near $48
Nothing, three peaks complete it
questions.why: A close under the $44 neckline. Until that line breaks, the uptrend isn't reversed.
questions.lesson_line: The neckline break is the signal. The shape alone is a warning.

wrong.A new high above $55: That would put price above the head. The top completes on a break lower.
wrong.A third peak near $48: There are already three peaks. The missing piece is the neckline break.
wrong.Nothing, three peaks complete it: The pattern isn't complete until the neckline breaks.

questions.q: Head at $60, neckline at $50. Measure head to neckline and subtract that from the neckline. What's the target?
questions.why: $40. The head sits $60 less $50 above the neckline; take that off the $50 neckline. Any target is a rough guide.
questions.lesson_line: Head-to-neckline height, projected down from the neckline. A guide, not a promise.

questions.story: A stock builds a flat floor at $30 with lower highs above it. Textbooks call the pattern bearish. You have no position.
questions.q: What's the disciplined move?
choices: Wait for a close outside a line
Short now, the pattern is bearish
Buy now, the floor will hold
Buy at the apex before it breaks
questions.answer: Wait for a close outside a line
questions.why: Wait for a close outside a line. Bulkowski's data has descending triangles breaking upward 53% of the time. A textbook bias isn't a breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Let the breakout pick the direction. The textbook bias doesn't.

wrong.Short now, the pattern is bearish: That's trading the bias. These can break either way, and the pattern isn't complete until support breaks.
wrong.Buy now, the floor will hold: Floors break too. Nothing is confirmed yet.
wrong.Buy at the apex before it breaks: That's still a guess before any breakout, and a break too close to the apex may mean little.

questions.story: A stock has traded between $20 and $25 for months. One day it drops to $19.40, then closes back at $20.60.
questions.q: In Wyckoff terms, which word fits?
choices: Spring
Breakdown
Double top
Pennant
questions.why: Spring. Price broke under the range's floor and quickly closed back inside it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring dips under support and snaps back inside. A breakdown stays down.

wrong.Breakdown: A breakdown stays below support. This closed back inside the range.
wrong.Double top: That's two peaks near the top of a range, not a dip under the floor.
wrong.Pennant: A pennant is a short triangle after a sharp run.

questions.q: What does shakeout mean?
choices: A sharp dip that scares holders out
A slow climb on steadily rising volume
A gap up on strong earnings news
A week of very tiny daily ranges
questions.answer: A sharp dip that scares holders out
questions.why: A sharp drop that scares holders out. Many investors sell at once, often at a loss, on fear or bad news.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout runs scared holders out, and it's usually fast.

wrong.A slow climb on steadily rising volume: That's buyers in control. Nobody is being scared out.
wrong.A gap up on strong earnings news: Holders are rewarded by that, not scared out.
wrong.A week of very tiny daily ranges: That's a quiet, tight market. A shakeout is sharp.

questions.q: In Wyckoff's method, what is the cause?
choices: The range's build-up behind a move
The news that started the big selloff
The breakout day's volume spike
The trend before the range began
questions.answer: The range's build-up behind a move
questions.why: The build-up inside the trading range. In Wyckoff's law of cause and effect, the range builds the cause and the move out of it is the effect.
questions.lesson_line: Wyckoff: the range builds the cause; the trend that follows is the effect.

wrong.The news that started the big selloff: News can start a move, but Wyckoff's cause is built inside the trading range.
wrong.The breakout day's volume spike: That's the move leaving the range, the start of the effect.
wrong.The trend before the range began: That trend comes before the range. The cause is built inside it.

questions.q: In Wyckoff's method, an accumulation range needs a spring.
questions.why: False. Springs and terminal shakeouts are not required. One Wyckoff accumulation schematic shows a spring and the other doesn't.
questions.lesson_line: No spring doesn't mean no base. It's optional.

questions.q: What does flat base mean?
choices: Sideways for several weeks or more
A steep, sudden run on heavy volume
A V-shaped drop and fast recovery
A gap that does not fill for weeks
questions.answer: Sideways for several weeks or more
questions.why: Sideways for several weeks or months. Bulkowski compares it to a rectangle: price keeps touching the same levels.
questions.lesson_line: Flat base: the stock moves sideways, neither up nor down, for weeks.

wrong.A steep, sudden run on heavy volume: That's a flagpole, the opposite of a base.
wrong.A V-shaped drop and fast recovery: A V is a sharp reversal. A base goes sideways.
wrong.A gap that does not fill for weeks: A gap is a jump between two bars, not a base.

questions.q: What does Darvas box mean?
choices: A box built from recent highs, lows
A rounded base with a short handle
A flat top with steadily rising lows
Three peaks, with the middle highest
questions.answer: A box built from recent highs, lows
questions.why: A range framed by recent highs and lows. The buy signal is a break above the top of the box.
questions.lesson_line: Darvas box: a top, a bottom, and a trade on the break.

questions.q: A pattern's measured target tells you how far price will go.
questions.why: False. Bulkowski calls the measure rule an estimate only, and usually inaccurate. StockCharts calls any target a rough guide.
questions.lesson_line: Targets are guides. Manage the trade on what price actually does.

questions.q: Once a cup with handle breaks out, price rarely gives much back.
questions.why: False. Fidelity's guide says these often have a throwback, a return to the breakout price. Bulkowski checked 300: 47% dropped substantially within two months.
questions.lesson_line: A clean breakout still needs a stop. Nearly half gave back a lot.

questions.story: You buy a cup with handle breakout at $50.10. The handle dipped to $47 before the breakout.
questions.q: Where does the textbook put your stop?
choices: Just under the handle's low
No stop until the target hits
Lower it if price gets close
questions.why: Just under the handle's low, near $47. Bulkowski names the handle low as a good stop, and Investopedia puts stops below the handle.
questions.lesson_line: Set the stop before you buy. The handle's low is the natural line.

wrong.No stop until the target hits: Hope isn't a stop. Bulkowski found 47% of these dropped substantially within two months of the breakout.
wrong.Lower it if price gets close: That widens the loss you planned for. Bulkowski's advice runs the other way: raise the stop as price rises.

questions.q: A head and shoulders top needs an uptrend in front of it.
questions.why: True. A reversal needs something to reverse. Without a prior uptrend there's no head and shoulders top.
questions.lesson_line: No uptrend before it, no head and shoulders top.

questions.story: After a long slide, a stock makes three lows: $30, then $26, then $30.50. The rally highs between them sit near $34.
questions.q: Which word fits?
choices: Inverse head and shoulders
Triple bottom
Double bottom
Head and shoulders top
questions.why: Inverse head and shoulders. The middle low is the deepest, and the two outer lows sit near the same level.
questions.lesson_line: Deep middle low, level lows either side: the bottom version of head and shoulders.

wrong.Triple bottom: A triple bottom's three lows sit at about the same price. Here the middle one is far lower.
wrong.Double bottom: There are three lows here, not two.
wrong.Head and shoulders top: A top is made of peaks, not lows.

questions.q: Which chart shows a rounding bottom best?
choices: The weekly chart
An intraday chart
A one-month daily chart
questions.why: The weekly chart. Rounding bottoms take many months, and Bulkowski says they're hard to spot unless you look on the weekly scale.
questions.lesson_line: Slow patterns need a zoomed-out chart. Check the weekly.

wrong.An intraday chart: Far too short. This pattern takes many months.
wrong.A one-month daily chart: A month barely covers part of the bowl.

questions.q: A shakeout does not always mean the uptrend is over; the prior trend often reasserts.
questions.why: True. Investopedia notes the prior trend often reasserts after a shakeout. In Wyckoff's method, shakeouts can come once an advance has started.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout is a scare, not a verdict. Often the prior trend reasserts.

questions.story: A stock breaks out of an ascending triangle at $40. It rises to $41.50, stalls, then closes below the triangle's low at $36.
questions.q: What does Bulkowski call this?
choices: A busted pattern
A throwback
A spring
questions.why: A busted pattern. Price moved less than 10% after the breakout, then closed through the other side. Fidelity's guide calls it a failed breakout.
questions.lesson_line: When a breakout fails and price exits the other side, respect it.

wrong.A throwback: A throwback comes back to the breakout level. This fell through the whole pattern.
wrong.A spring: A spring dips under support and closes back inside. This closed below and stayed there.

questions.story: You bought a flag breakout. Its measured target is $38. Price stalls at $36, then the whole market sells off hard.
questions.q: Do you hold on for the $38 target?
choices: No, reassess: conditions changed
Yes, the target is the plan
Yes, and add to get there faster
questions.why: No, reassess. Fidelity's pattern guide lists sticking with an original target after conditions change as a dangerous habit. Bulkowski calls targets an estimate only.
questions.lesson_line: The target was an estimate made earlier. Trade what's in front of you now.

wrong.Yes, the target is the plan: A target is an estimate, not a promise from the market.
wrong.Yes, and add to get there faster: Adding into a selloff to chase a target doubles down on an estimate.

questions.story: A stock forms what looks like an inverse head and shoulders. It's at $33, just under its $34 neckline. A friend wants to buy now to get in early.
questions.q: What does the textbook say?
choices: Wait for the close above $34
Buy now, the shape is done
Buy half now, half at $34
questions.why: Wait for the close above $34. Bulkowski says wait for confirmation, and Schwab notes many investors have paid a steep price for trading before it.
questions.lesson_line: Early is a guess. The neckline break is the signal.

wrong.Buy now, the shape is done: A shape isn't a pattern until it breaks out.
wrong.Buy half now, half at $34: Half a position bought on a guess is still a guess.

questions.q: An ascending triangle can still break down.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski counts upward breakouts 63% of the time, not always. Fidelity's guide says it can break either way, more often up.
questions.lesson_line: Bullish bias, not a guarantee. Plan for the break you don't expect.

questions.q: Wedges rank among the best-performing chart patterns.
questions.why: False. Bulkowski calls rising wedges some of the worst performers and the falling wedge a poor one. Fidelity's guide rates both below average.
questions.lesson_line: A pattern's fame isn't its record. Wedges test poorly.

questions.q: What separates a symmetrical triangle from a pennant?
choices: A pennant is short, after a sharp run
Pennants have two parallel lines
Triangles need a long downtrend first
Pennants come with no flagpole
questions.answer: A pennant is short, after a sharp run
questions.why: Pennants are short and follow a sharp move. A symmetrical triangle can form without one and runs longer. StockCharts calls one under three weeks a pennant.
questions.lesson_line: Same shape, different setting: a pennant hangs off a pole.

wrong.Pennants have two parallel lines: Parallel lines make a flag. A pennant's lines converge, like a triangle's.
wrong.Triangles need a long downtrend first: The trend into a symmetrical triangle can be either direction.
wrong.Pennants come with no flagpole: It's the reverse. A pennant needs a sharp move, its pole, before it.

questions.q: Which word is this: three roughly equal highs, then a break below the lows between them.
choices: Triple top
Head and shoulders
Double top
Ascending triangle
questions.why: Triple top. Three tries at the same ceiling fail, and the break of the lows between them completes it.
questions.lesson_line: Triple top: three equal highs, done only when support breaks.

wrong.Head and shoulders: Its middle peak is higher than the other two.
wrong.Ascending triangle: Its flat top comes with rising lows, and its bias is bullish.

questions.q: Which word is this: price pokes above a range's top, then quickly closes back inside the range.
choices: Upthrust
Spring
Breakout
Throwback
questions.why: Upthrust. It's the spring turned upside down: a quick push above resistance that fails and closes back in the range.
questions.lesson_line: Upthrust above the range, spring below it. Both fail and snap back.

wrong.Spring: A spring dips below the range's floor, not above its top.
wrong.Breakout: A breakout holds outside the range. This closed back inside.
wrong.Throwback: A throwback is a return to the breakout level after a breakout that held.

conflicts: Double bottom lows: StockCharts accepts a second low within 3% of the first, Investopedia within 3% to 4%, Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slides 'roughly the same price'. IBD's double bottom (O'Neil) wants the second low to UNDERCUT the first, and Bulkowski's 'ugly double bottom' has the second low 5% to 15% HIGHER. q40 asks only the computed gap and StockCharts' 3% reading of 'roughly equal'; no question says the second low must undercut or must sit higher. IBD's undercut rule could not be quoted: investors.com shows this client only each article's first paragraph.

Descending triangle direction: StockCharts calls it bearish and Fidelity's guide says it breaks 'most commonly downward'; Bulkowski's current table says upward 53% of the time. No question keys a direction; q44 keys the point all three allow (wait for the close outside a line) and names both readings in the reveal.

Flag and pennant length: StockCharts' flag article says one to 12 weeks (ideally one to four), its glossary says flags 'generally' last under three weeks, Bulkowski says under three weeks, Investopedia's pennant page one to three weeks. No question keys a length. q31 uses a four-month flag, past both StockCharts' 12 weeks and Bulkowski's three, so both call it a rectangle (checker: it said 'for months', and StockCharts still calls a two-month flag a flag).
Cup length: Bulkowski and Investopedia give 7 to 65 weeks; StockCharts and Fidelity's indicator guide say one to six months. Not asked.

Cup with handle entry: IBD uses the handle's highest price plus 10 cents; Investopedia a buy stop slightly above the handle's upper trend line (or a close above it); Fidelity's guide a break through the cup's right side; Bulkowski a close above the right cup rim, or an earlier close above a down-sloping handle trendline. q27 keys the shared part, 'just above the top of the handle'.

Cup with handle stop: Bulkowski names the handle low; Investopedia allows below the handle or below the cup; Bulkowski's throwback study prefers two cents under the breakout day's low followed by a volatility stop. q53 keys the handle low (both Bulkowski and Investopedia allow it) and offers no other legitimate stop as a wrong choice.

Spring volume: the Wyckoff tutorial (StockCharts / Wyckoff Analytics) reads a LOW-volume spring as a sign the stock is ready to rise; the CMT Association's 'Reversal Bars' piece says volume on a spring is 'typically quite high (the higher the better)'. No question mentions volume on a spring; q45's story gives none.

Spring sources: the StockCharts ChartSchool Wyckoff tutorial and the Wyckoff Analytics page carry the same text (StockCharts republishes it). The spring definition questions also rest on independently worded definitions: StockCharts' glossary entry and the CMT Association piece. The cause question (q47) now also cites independently written slides by Hank Pruden hosted by the CMT Association (s57, checker). q48 (springs are optional) still rests on the shared tutorial text alone (StockCharts plus Wyckoff Analytics, the method's own school); the checker's search found no other reliable source, only vendor blogs.

Saucer: StockCharts (article and glossary) and Bulkowski ('saucer lip') use saucer for the rounding bottom. Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slide titles the cup and handle 'Cup and Handle (also Saucer)'. q20 keys the StockCharts/Bulkowski usage.
Rounding bottom: StockCharts treats it as a reversal after a decline; Bulkowski finds price trending UP into it 67% of the time (acting as a continuation). Not asked.

Head and shoulders target: StockCharts, Fidelity and Schwab project the full head-to-neckline height; Bulkowski multiplies it by his 'percentage meeting price target' (51% for tops). q43 asks the textbook full-height method and calls it a rough guide.

Wedge touches: StockCharts asks for at least two reaction highs (ideally three) and two reaction lows; Bulkowski and Fidelity's guide want at least five touches (three on one line, two on the other). q33 names Bulkowski and Fidelity.

Pullback: Bulkowski and Fidelity's slides use 'pullback' for a return to the breakout price after a DOWNWARD breakout; V.02 teaches the everyday meaning (a dip in an uptrend). This unit does not ask the pattern-book meaning.

Shakeout: StockCharts' glossary and Investopedia define it broadly (many investors exit at once); the Wyckoff tutorial describes shakeouts engineered by large operators. Investopedia says the word is used almost only for an interruption in a longer uptrend, but the Wyckoff tutorial says shakeouts 'may also' come once an advance has started and StockCharts' glossary example is the dot-com bust, a decline. So no question says shakeouts usually come in uptrends: q46 keys the broad meaning; q57 (rewritten by the checker) keys only that a shakeout does not by itself mean the uptrend is over (Investopedia: the prior trend often reasserts; Wyckoff: shakeouts inside an advance).
